generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, self-efficacy decides whether you keep going on the parts that feel hard, such as leading a session or coding match data. Believing you can handle a specific task grows as you master small pieces of it. Motivation matters too. A student who works to understand their subject tends to outlast one who works only for the next mark, especially when the task is demanding. Across the school, that demanding task might be a biomechanics analysis, a coaching assessment or a rehab case, but self-belief and the right motivation carry all of them.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students face the same demanding task: an assessed coaching session they must plan and lead with a real group.

Tom is driven mainly by the grade and has little belief that he can hold a group's attention. The first ragged drill confirms the fear, so he decides there is no point preparing further and leads a thin, underprepared session. Low self-belief and a focus on the grade alone made the task easy to give up on.

Amara also finds it daunting, but starts by rehearsing one drill until it runs smoothly, then a second, building a sense that she can do this. She wants to become a better coach, not just pass, so she watches an experienced coach and asks how they manage a restless group. Self-belief and learning motivation keep her effort going to the end.

Both students found the task hard. Only Amara built the self-efficacy, and drew on the motivation, needed to lead it well.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, what keeps you going on hard work is self-belief and the right kind of motivation. Self-efficacy is your belief that you can do a specific task, such as leading a session, and it grows through mastery, seeing others succeed, feedback and managing nerves. Learning motivation sustains effort better than chasing marks alone. You can now tell the two motivations apart and build self-efficacy on purpose. The last lesson turns this into goals.

check.body: In the worked example, how did Amara build self-efficacy for the coaching session?

items.text: By rehearsing one drill until it ran smoothly, then another, and watching an experienced coach.
By reminding herself that the grade was all that mattered.
By deciding that holding a group was simply not for her.
By leading a thin, underprepared session to get it over with.

feedback.correct: That's right. Mastering small parts and seeing someone succeed built Amara's self-efficacy.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the moves that gave Amara a sense of being able to do it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara built self-efficacy by rehearsing one drill then another, and by watching an experienced coach. The others describe low self-belief.
